On the basis of testimony of prosecution witness (PW1) on 21.07.2008 charge was framed against the appellant/accused for commission of offences punishable u/s 7/16(1A) of PFA Act for violation of provisions of Sub clause 2(i)(ia)(j) of PFA Act alleging therein that on 16.12.2004 at about 05:15 p.m. appellant/ accused being the Vendor cum Proprietor of M/s Royal Caterers, Khasra No. 1012,
Prem Nagar-II, Kirari, Delhi was found present at the given premises and conducting business of food article and sold for analysis sample of Sela Rice of approximately 1500 grams taken from an open small gunny bag having no label declaration which was meant for human consumption and it was analyzed by the Director CFL vide Certificate no. 63/LHA/10737 dated 30.04.2005 and found that the sample is adulterated as there was presence of synthetic colour i.e. tartrazine + Sunset yellow FCF and thereby violated the provisions of Section 2(i)(ia) (j) of PFA Act, 1954 punishable under section 16(1A) of PFA Act, 1954 read with Section 7 of the PFA Act to which he pleaded not guilty and claimed trial.

sentences.text: The appellant was accordingly convicted and sentenced by the learned trial court and aggrieved by the said judgment and order on quantum of sentence dated 30.08.2016, the present appeal has been preferred by the appellant.
9.(I) The appellant has assailed the judgment and order on sentence passed by the learned trial court by urging various grounds.

II) Alternatively, on the quantum of sentence, relying upon the new legislation, it was pleaded that the case of the appellant be considered sympathetically in the light of the preposition of law laid down by the Hon'ble Courts pursuant to coming of new legislation that is Food Safety & Standards Act.

10. During the course of argument on 05.03.2021, learned counsel for the appellant submitted that appellant is not challenging the merits of the case/ conviction decided by the learned trial court vide judgment dated 24.08.2016, and is confining his appeal limited to the quantum of sentence only awarded to him vide order dated 30.08.2016 ; and to affirm his submissions, appellant has tender his affidavit duly sworn and notarized by the Oath Commissioner in that regard and prayed that a lenient view be taken against him by giving him the benefit of New Legislation as FSSAI.
11.

Learned counsel for the Delhi Admn./Food Department, objected to the same and submitted that according to submission of CA no. 8729/16 Ajay Kr. Gupta @ Ajay Kumar Vs. Food Inspector (PFA)
pages 6 of 13 appellant, prosecution has established its case and he be sentenced with strict punishment in terms of old Act wherein minimum punishment is prescribed and no leniency should be shown to the convict as it is a serious offence of food adulteration article / commodity leading to hazardous consequences on the health or body of a person.
12.

sentences.text: I have carefully gone through the available record as well as trial court record, have heard the submissions of learned counsel for both the parties at length and have also gone through the judgments relied upon by the parties.

13. In light of above submissions and discussion particularly when the affidavit of appellant to this effect is filed on record, I find no valid and legal reasons to interfere with the well reasoned judgment of the learned trial court.
The findings of the learned trial court with respect to the conviction of the appellant for the offence punishable under 16(1A) of the PFA Act read with Section 7 of the PFA Act, 1954 are upheld.
II. Now Coming to the alternate plea of giving benefit of new legislation to the appellant/ accused.
14. It is argued by learned counsel for the appellant that on the date of pronouncement of judgment/order on sentence, the PFA Act, 1954 was repealed and new act has thereafter come into operation.

It is stated that the court should give benefit of the new legislation to the accused vide which the punishment provided under the old act has been diluted to a considerable extent, and that Ajay Kumar Gupta vs Delhi Admn/Food Inspector on 5 March, 2021 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/189032825/
4

the offence for which the accused/appellant has been convicted now falls under the CA no. 8729/16 Ajay Kr. Gupta @ Ajay Kumar Vs. Food Inspector (PFA) pages 7 of 13 category of "Unsafe Food"
punishable under section 59(1) of the new Act i.e Food and Safety Standards Act, 2006 (hereinafter called FSSAI) punishable upto six months and fine of upto Rs. One lac only.

15. It was argued by learned counsel for the appellant that appellant is a man of 45 years of age,
respectable person of society, has deep roots in the society, running a small Kiryana shop for livelihood of his family consisting of wife, one son and one daughter and old aged parents who are suffering from various old age ailments, has duties and responsibilities towards his family, not involved in any other case,
and prayed that a lenient view be taken against him in the light of the provisions of law under the new Act.

15.1 Further it is stated that case pertains to the year 2004, the appellant/accused has faced the trial almost 17 years which by itself is a sufficient punishment and,
the hardships faced by him has caused him great mental agony, stress and rigors of trial during the said period.

It is also stated that now a days special circumstances exists due to outbreak of pandemic of Covid-19 and there are chances of appellant being infected with virus in case imprisonment of sentence is awarded to him.

15.2 In support of his submissions qua the consideration of the case under new legislation, learned counsel for appellant had relied upon the judgment of Nemi Chand Vs. State of Rajasthan ( Crl.
Appeals No. 214 and 215 of 2016, vide order dated 10.03.2016, as corrected vide order dated 17.03.2016, as reported in 2016 (1) FAC 203 ) of Hon'ble Supreme Court and earlier judgment T Barai CA no. 8729/16 Ajay Kr. Gupta @ Ajay Kumar Vs. Food Inspector (PFA) pages 8 of 13 Vs.
Henry 1983 ( ) SCC 177.
15.3

sentences.text: Per contra, learned SPP, strongly opposed the submissions advanced by learned counsel by addressing that the sentencing cannot be done in new Act since the definition of many offences have changed in the new Act including this particular offence of which accused is charged.
Definition of major offences like "adulteration" and "misbranding" have been changed.
Now FSSAI have definition "substandard food", "food containing extraneous matter" "unsafe food" and misbranded food".
Due to this reason, the ingredients have changed and thus there is no way in which the old offences could be related to new offences.
15.4 In the present case, the offence was that the food article i.e. Sela Rice was found adulterated and was unfit for human consumption.

This was violation of Rules under PFA Rules and thus termed as adulteration in view of Section 2(ia) (j) of the PFA Act and thus consequently punishable under section 16(1A) of PFA Act read with Section 7 of PFA Act.
15.5
That now in the FSSAI such adulteration is termed as "unsafe food" in terms of Section 3(zz)(viii) of FSSA Act and violation thereof is punishable u/s 59(1) of FSSA.
So if we go through both these provisions of law a particular offence with a particular fact is mentioned with some other name but with same ingredients in the New FSSA Act.

- Sub-clause (viii) of 3(zz) FSSA Act is applicable where the colouring material or the preservative other than that specified in respect there of is found in the food article and not where the CA no.

sentences.text: 15.6 Further, the charge in this case was framed for the said offences and there is no charge in which it is stated that the said adulteration was injuries to health.

Had it been the case, the charge would have been for the offence punishable u/s 16(1-A)(ii) of PFA Act r/w section 2(ia)(l) & (f).
15.7
Thus, it is held that it is the ingredients which constitute an offence and determines whether it is the same offence but with new name or an altogether different offence,

Here the offence of adding colour in the food article which was punishable u/s 16(1)(a) PFA Act is similar to the offence u/s 59 of FSSAI Act, which is now punishable with simple imprisonment of six months and fine upto one lakh.
15.8 Now, coming to the application of Nemi Chand Judgment (supra), the same is based on the old judgment i.e. T Barai ( Supra) of Hon'ble Supreme Court.

The relevant portion of the T Barai Judgment is as follows :
- (Para 25) It is settled both on authority and principle that when a later statute again describes an offence created by an earlier statute and imposes a different punishment or varies the procedure, the earlier statute is repealed by implication in Michell Vs.
Brown ( 1958) 120 ER 909, 912 : 32 LTOS 146:7 WR 80 Lord Campbell put the matter thus :
- "It is well settled rule of construction that, if a later statute again describes an ofence created by a former statute and affixes a different punishment, varying the procedure, the earlier statute is CA no. 8729/16 Ajay Kr. Gupta @ Ajay Kumar Vs.
Food Inspector (PFA) pages 10 of 13 repealed by the later statute see also Smith Vs.
Benabo ( 1937) 1 ALL ER 523 : ( 1997) 1 KB 518: 156 LT 194"
- In Regina Vs. Youle ( 1861) 158 ER 311,315-16 : LT 299 : 9 WR 637 Martin B. said in the oft-quoted passage :
- If a statute deals with a particular class of offences, and a subsequent Act is passed which deals with precisely the same offence, and a different punishment is imposed by the later Act, I think that, in effect, the legislature has declared that the new Act shall be substituted for the earlier Act."

Food Inspector (PFA) pages 11 of 13 in Nemi Chand's Case (supra) issued an advisory to the Commissioners of Food Safety/Officers incharge of Food Safety to dispose of the long pending court cases filed under old PFA Act mainly concerning substandard and misbranding by imposing fine only.

sentences.text:
15-B - In view of the above mentioned discussion, it can be safely said that while considering the point of sentence, in backdrop of the object and reasons of the act and the intention of the legislature, the quantum of sentence so passed in the interest of justice needs to be considered under the new Act i.e. FSSAI, while deciding the present appeal.
16.

Thus, analyzing the facts of the case, taking note of the special circumstances of the case and the fact that accused has faced the trial of almost 16 years ; in light of the above cited judgment and the judgment of Hon'ble High Court of Delhi titled as GNCT Vs. Jagdish Tyagi dated 11.10.2017 in my view the convict/ appellant is entitled to the benefit of new legislation.

Accordingly to meet the ends of justice, the sentence of the convict Ajay Kumar Gupta as imposed by the learned trial court vide order dated 30.08.2016 stands modified to the extent that the order sentencing the appellant to undergo simple imprisonment of two years stands waived off to simple imprisonment for one day i.e. till rising of the court ; the sentence of fine is enhanced from Rs. 2,00,000/- to Rs. 4,00,000/- In default of payment of fine the appellant/convict shall undergo simple imprisonment for two months.
Sentence modified accordingly.

- The rule is however subject to the limitation contained in Article 20(1) against ex post facto law providing for a greater punishment and has also no application where the offence described in the later Act is not the same as in the earlier Act i.e. when the essential ingredients of the two offences are different.
15-B - In view of the above mentioned discussion, it can be safely said that while considering the point of sentence, in backdrop of the object and reasons of the act and the intention of the legislature, the quantum of sentence so passed in the interest of justice needs to be considered under the new Act i.e. FSSAI, while deciding the present appeal.
16.
